The Bottom Line on MRVL Stock

Marvell has set a bold financial target, raising expectations. Its stock trades at 56 times projected 2027 earnings, so investors are paying a premium for the hope of higher growth in the future. This also puts MRVL stock at risk if growth slows or the company does not meet its lofty goals. The recent rebound is an encouraging sign, but the next earnings reports will show whether the company is making progress toward management's goals.

news.Title: Europe's financial regulators query Google over cloud outage that hit banks
news.Content:
By Phoebe Seers and Elizabeth Howcroft

LONDON/PARIS, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Financial regulators in Europe are questioning Google after a cloud computing outage on Tuesday left millions of bank customers without access to ‌key financial services for hours.

The European Banking Authority said that it has been in contact with ‌Google Cloud to obtain further information on the incident, understand its implications and assess its potential impact on financial entities in the ​EU, a spokesperson for the watchdog told Reuters.

Alphabet's Google said the disruption, which lasted several hours, was caused by a "power event" in a London-based network that serves customers across Europe. Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC were among the banks affected.

Lloyds and HSBC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A Google spokesperson said: "We have resolved a disruption to ‌Google Cloud services at a third-party ⁠facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis."

At Revolut, which has around ⁠13 million UK customers, a wide range of services including logging in, card payments and cash withdrawals were affected on Tuesday, according to the bank's website.

Revolut said in a statement that it was reviewing the incident to reduce the impact ​of ​any future third-party disruptions, and that customer funds and data ​had remained safe throughout.

The outage is the ‌first major test of new rules across Europe designed to strengthen the resilience of technology providers, including cloud firms, on which the financial sector depends.

The European Union last year designated 19 technology firms as critical third-party providers to the financial sector, bringing them under joint direct oversight of three financial regulators — including the EBA — for the first time. Britain took similar steps for four cloud providers, citing the risk that an outage at a ‌major supplier could affect multiple financial firms at the same ​time. Google Cloud falls under both regulatory frameworks.

In Britain, parliament's Treasury ​Committee has written to the Bank of England ​and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), seeking details of the regulators' response to the outage ‌on Tuesday, the scale of the disruption and ​any financial harm caused.

The FCA ​said it was engaging with Google over the incident. Under Britain's critical third party regime, designated providers like Google Cloud must report serious outages to the FCA and the BoE.

Story Continues

A spokesperson for the Bank ​of England declined to comment.

Under UK ‌rules, banks ultimately are responsible for the services they provide to customers, including when they ​rely on third-party providers.

(Reporting by Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Phoebe Seers in London; additional reporting ​by Lawrence White in London; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

Still, on the second-quarter earnings call, management increased its full-year revenue guidance to $91.2 billion and specifically said that adjusted operating profit would be about $8.65 billion.

Why the guidance change isn't good news

Superficially, it's an increase in revenue guidance and also an increase over the implied guidance of $8.611 billion I calculated above. However, there are two key considerations for investors, and they matter a lot for the upcoming results of a company with a near-7% dividend yield .

First, the new guidance implies an adjusted operating margin of 9.48%, down from the 9.6% initially forecast. Second, it's important to understand the nuance of the guidance change. Bearing in mind that the increase in full-year revenue guidance was $1.5 billion to $91.2 billion, it's reasonable to expect a large chunk of the revenue increase is due to the fuel surcharge.

It passed 30 million paid seats in the fiscal fourth quarter. Azure, Microsoft's cloud, rents computing power and AI models to businesses, and its revenue grew 43% in that quarter. Microsoft also holds a financial stake in OpenAI, whose products run on Azure first.

Microsoft sells new AI tools faster than most rivals because its software already runs inside almost every large company, so customers skip the long process of approving a new vendor. Its commercial backlog, which is signed business not yet delivered, rose 84%, or 25% without OpenAI. See whether the spending is paying off.

Will AI Agents Replace the Office Seat?

This is the biggest worry on the software side. Most of Microsoft's revenue and profit still come from software sold per user. If AI agents do office work, companies need fewer employee seats, and Microsoft itself expects seat growth to slow over time. Microsoft has three answers. Companies need cloud computing to run AI agents, and Azure rents it out. Its customers' work data already sits in Microsoft's systems, which AI agents need to do useful work. Microsoft is also building its own AI models, expected by 2027, to cut what it pays outside AI providers when people use Copilot.

Chips are the second. Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 AI chip this month and says it delivers 40% more output per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. Production starts early next year. The chip could reduce Microsoft's reliance on Nvidia, but earlier Maia versions shipped only in limited volumes.

OpenAI is the third. It makes up a large part of the backlog, which is why the 84% growth drops to 25% without it. A change in that relationship would hit Microsoft's AI sales.

If Azure grows 44% to 45% or faster and Microsoft shows Copilot use deepening, the rally has support. If Azure lands on guidance but capital spending rises faster than cash flow and Microsoft gives no new Copilot data, the stock could stall, since expectations have moved up. If Azure growth falls short, capacity limits persist or OpenAI news hits the backlog, the AI-spending worry that sent shares down after the fiscal 2026 third-quarter report could return. The market expects Microsoft (MSFT) to deliver a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.

Estimate Revisions Trend

The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.35% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.

Investors should keep in mind that an aggregate change may not always reflect the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Earnings Whisper

Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.

How Have the Numbers Shaped Up for Microsoft?

Bottom Line

An earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss.

That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. news.Content:
United Parcel Service UPS is scheduled to report its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 27, before the market opens. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the to-be-reported quarter's earnings per share and revenues is pegged at $1.63 and $22.23 billion, respectively.

For 2026, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for UPS' revenues is pegged at $91.71 billion, implying a 3.4% year-over-year uptick. The consensus mark for 2026 EPS is pegged at $7.19, indicating a year-over-year improvement of 0.4%.

This package delivery company's earnings beat estimates each of the past four quarters, with the average surprise being 12.4%.

United Parcel Service, Inc. Price and EPS Surprise

Q3 Earnings Whispers for UPS

Our proven model predicts an earnings beat for UPS for the September quarter. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold) increases the odds of an earnings beat. That is exactly the case here. You can uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they're reported with our Earnings ESP Filter.

UPS has an Earnings ESP of +0.95% and a Zacks Rank #3. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here.

Factors Shaping UPS' Quarterly Performance

We expect the still-ongoing macro uncertainty due to the Middle East conflict to have dented UPS' performance in the September quarter. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has resulted in a sharp jump in oil prices. This has been naturally hurting the bottom line of transportation stocks, like UPS. This is because fuel expenses represent a key input cost for a transportation company.

UPS' decision to scale back business with Amazon AMZN is expected to have kept third-quarter volumes muted. Management reached an agreement in principle with Amazon to reduce the e-commerce giant's volume by more than 50% by June 2026. CEO Carol Tome noted that Amazon was not the company's most profitable customer. The reduction in volumes is compelling UPS to right-size its network. We expect overall volumes to decline 5.4% year over year in the September quarter.

That said, third-quarter results are likely to reflect UPS' efforts toward improving profitability over sheer volume, through its "Better, Not Bigger" strategy. Under the cost-cutting initiatives, UPS has substantially reduced its U.S. operational workforce and closed daily operations at multiple leased and owned buildings. Moreover, UPS has been focusing on increasing automation in sorting and operations and leveraging AI for logistics planning to boost efficiency.

Story Continues

The shift in focus toward higher-margin areas such as small and medium-sized businesses or SMBs and healthcare logistics from low-margin volumes (like Amazon) is expected to be reflected in UPS' first-quarter results. Notably, SMBs contributed 34.5% to total U.S. volume in the June quarter, reflecting a 250-basis-point year-over-year improvement. We expect SMBs to have performed strongly in the September quarter as well, boosting results.

UPS Underperforms on Price Front

Shares of UPS have declined marginally year to date ("YTD"), similar to the Zacks Transportation-Air Freight and Cargo industry. Shares of rival FedEx FDX have seen a single-digit (% -wise) rise in the same timeframe.

YTD Price Comparison

On the basis of the forward 12-month Price/Sales (P/S), UPS' shares are trading at a discount compared with the industry average. FedEx is cheaper. UPS and FedEx each currently have a Value Score of B.

Investment Thesis for UPS Stock

UPS is looking to grow its per-package revenues by gaining more business in segments like healthcare. A few years back, UPS acquired Bomi Group, an industry-leading multinational healthcare logistics provider. Last year, UPS acquired Andlauer Healthcare Group as part of its commitment to offer global specialty capabilities.

Because of this strategic shift, UPS did not increase its quarterly dividend this year, keeping it at $6.56 annually. In the event of the company failing to put an end to its struggles through the strategic shift, the high payout ratio may lead to a dividend cut, which would be disastrous for dividend investors.

End Note

It is worth noting that the company has the brand and the network to continue generating steady cash flows in the long run. This makes UPS a compelling long-term player in the transportation space. However, the near-term headwinds, including the macro uncertainties and volume declines, are hard to ignore.

So, all in all, it is worth holding on to UPS stock for now. Betting on the stock ahead of its upcoming results does not seem like a good idea. It is better to wait for management's commentary on volumes and cost-cutting efforts, apart from the updated 2026 guidance, to get more clarity on near-term prospects.

news.Title: Can Netlist's New LIGHTNING ULL DDR5 Boost Its AI Market Reach?
news.Content:
Netlist Inc . NLST recently announced next-generation LIGHTNING Ultra-Low Latency ("ULL") DDR5 RDIMMs for Agentic AI workstations and servers. The DDR5-6000 and DDR5-6400 products are designed to boost responsiveness in memory-sensitive AI and enterprise workloads.

The latest modules feature a JEDEC-compatible "drop-in architecture" supporting qualified deployments on AMD and Intel server platforms.

Netlist highlighted that internal testing demonstrated up to 10% lower loaded memory latency compared with conventional DDR5 RDIMMs, potentially improving performance in latency-sensitive applications.

The new products target agentic AI workstations and servers, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, large language models and vector databases. Applications also extend to high-frequency trading, scientific computing and electronic design automation, cloud infrastructure and data analytics.

Netlist remains focused on portfolio expansion to boost its presence in the AI memory market. On the last earnings call, management highlighted that its Lightning portfolio of overclocked, low-latency DDR5 RDIMM and UDIMM products has been gaining traction. Meanwhile, NLST's CXL NVvault solution is sampling with system-on-chip vendors, hyperscalers and key OEMs for next-generation hardware platforms. Netlist is also upbeat about MRDIMM and high-performance server memory architecture aimed at overcoming the bandwidth limitations of DDR5 RDIMMs. Management, citing industry analysts, noted that MRDIMM could be a $100 billion market by 2030.

Meanwhile, agreements with Micron MU and Samsung also strengthen its IP monetization strategy. The five-year licensing arrangement with Micron provides for $600 million in payments, beginning in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The LIGHTNING expansion could strengthen Netlist's position in AI infrastructure space, although wider adoption and meaningful revenue contributions remain key to its long-term growth prospects amid increasing competition in the semiconductor space.

Competitive Landscape

Netlist operates in a highly competitive memory market alongside established players, including Micron, Samsung Electronics, SK hynix SKHY and Rambus RMBS. While Netlist has recently strengthened its ties with Micron and Samsung through licensing agreements, competition in advanced AI memory technologies remains intense. Rambus represents another notable competitive force, offering DDR5 RDIMM and MRDIMM interface chipsets for data-center applications.

Last month, Micron demonstrated a 512GB DDR5 RDIMM capable of speeds up to 9,200 MT/s.

Story Continues

A few days back, Rambus unveiled a Power Management IC ("PMIC") solution. PMIC is designed to facilitate low-power, high-performance LPDDR6 Small Outline Compression Attached Memory Modules (SOCAMM2). Earlier in the year, Rambus expanded its DDR5 portfolio with complete DDR5-9600 chipsets for both client and server memory modules.

South Korea-based SK hynix has a strong presence across DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory ("HBM") markets. Recently, SK hynix showcased its next-generation AI memory portfolio, including 256GB DDR5 3DS RDIMM and 128GB DDR5 MRDIMM and 192GB SOCAMM2, at the OCP Global Summit 2026.The company also unveiled the second-generation 256GB CMM-DDR5 solution, offering approximately 30% better energy efficiency and more than twice the bandwidth than its predecessor.

news.Title: CIEN Wins Space Norway Cable Deal: Can Subsea Networking Drive Growth?
news.Content:
Ciena Corporation CIEN is strengthening its position in the global subsea networking market after securing a turnkey contract from Space Norway to modernize existing subsea cable systems in Svalbard and deploy advanced networking technology for the upcoming Arctic Way system. The project highlights the growing importance of resilient, high-capacity communications infrastructure in remote regions where connectivity is essential for scientific research, government operations and national security.

The agreement combines upgrades to legacy infrastructure with the deployment of a new subsea network expected to enter service in 2028. By supplying optical networking equipment, advanced transponders and network management software, Ciena aims to improve capacity, reliability and operational efficiency across Space Norway's Arctic communications footprint. For Ciena, this approach creates an opportunity to supply technology across multiple routes and potentially support future network extensions.

A key aspect of the deal is Ciena's combination of optical transmission hardware and network management software. The technology is designed to improve network capacity, simplify operations and support reliable data transmission across demanding subsea routes. Ciena 6500 Optical Platform provides optical transport capabilities for high-capacity networks. In the Arctic project, it will support communications across the new and upgraded subsea systems. Its Navigator Network Control Suite also provides visibility and control, helping Space Norway manage operations across its infrastructure while supporting operational redundancy.

The Space Norway agreement fuels Ciena's already strong business momentum, driven by increasing demand for high-speed connectivity and AI infrastructure. Ciena reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $1.67 billion, representing 37% year-over-year growth. It also raised its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to $6.42 billion (+/-$50 million). For fiscal 2027, management expects at least 30% revenue growth.

CIEN's Optical Growth Faces Competitive Challenges

CIEN continues to strengthen its position in the optical networking market as rising demand for high-capacity connectivity drives investments in digital infrastructure. Recently, Openreach deployed Ciena's Waveserver platform with WaveLogic 6 1.6Tb/s technology to expand its OSEA portfolio, offering high-capacity connectivity across U.K. cable landing stations, data centers and core network nodes. The solution combines 400G and 800G traffic over 1.6Tb/s wavelengths, supporting up to 32 400G services in a compact 2RU chassis.

Story Continues

However, Ciena operates in a competitive optical networking market. Winning contracts does not automatically guarantee attractive margins, especially when turnkey delivery involves substantial execution responsibilities. It faces competition from other optical networking vendors like Corning Incorporated GLW, Cisco Systems CSCO and Nokia NOK.

Assessing CIEN's Market Peers

Cisco's vertically integrated networking stack is expanding across scale-out and scale-across AI architectures. In the fiscal fourth quarter, it won three new hyperscaler designs – a P200 scale-across system, a G200 scale-out system and an optical line system. Fiscal 2026 hyperscaler AI orders were about 60% Silicon One-based systems and 40% optics, while Acacia generated more than $1 billion in orders in the fiscal fourth quarter. Management has line of sight to multiple additional design wins over the next six months across G300, G200 and P200 systems and optics. In September, management said Cisco supplies chips and full systems to hyperscalers and plans to become independent of merchant silicon providers by fiscal 2029, giving it greater control over product design and supply.

However, the outlook still depends on converting G300, G200, P200 and optics opportunities, and becoming independent of merchant silicon providers by fiscal 2029.

Corning has entered the second half of 2026 with its growth outlook tied to AI infrastructure and optical connectivity. It launched Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 and continues to see opportunities in advanced optics products tied to AI-driven data center build-outs and semiconductor manufacturing demand. Corning is also expanding its GenAI optical portfolio with multicore fiber and high-density connectivity solutions that improve network capacity and reduce installation complexity. Secular demand for bandwidth, cloud computing and AI infrastructure continues to support Corning's Optical Communications business.

GLW also announced a long-term partnership with NVIDIA to expand U.S.-based optical connectivity manufacturing capacity by 10 times and increase domestic fiber production capacity by more than 50%. In September, Corning secured a multiyear, multibillion-dollar agreement with Verizon to supply more than 80 million miles of high-density optical fiber and connectivity solutions through 2032, strengthening its long-term revenue visibility and positioning it to benefit from expanding broadband and AI infrastructure demand.

Nokia continues to benefit from its broad portfolio spanning mobile networks, optical transport, IP routing, fixed broadband, software and services. This integrated offering enables the company to address evolving customer requirements across telecommunications operators, enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers. Network Infrastructure delivered double-digit growth in second-quarter 2026, supported by continued momentum in Optical Networks and IP Networks. The planned divestiture of the Fixed Wireless Access CPE business simplifies the portfolio and allows greater investment in higher-growth opportunities such as AI networking and optical technologies.

While AI and cloud demand is supporting Optical Networks and IP Networks, carrier spending remains mixed across regions and business lines. Management continues to expect stronger performance in the second half of 2026, but quarterly demand patterns remain influenced by customer capital expenditure timing and software revenue recognition. Management noted that supply constraints continue to affect portions of the optical networking market, contributing to long-term customer ordering patterns.

news.Title: AEIS Rides on Strong Semiconductor Growth: Can It Beat KLAC and MKSI?
news.Content:
Advanced Energy AEIS benefits from strong demand for semiconductor equipment, driven by increasing investments in advanced logic and memory manufacturing. The company's growing adoption of precision power solutions and expanding product portfolio strengthen its competitive position against KLA KLAC and MKS MKSI, which are also benefiting from semiconductor industry growth.

The company reported record semiconductor revenues of $278 million in the second quarter of 2026, increasing 33% year over year and 27% sequentially. Growth was driven by robust demand for leading-edge memory and logic technologies, alongside rising etch and deposition intensity. Management expects semiconductor revenues to increase nearly 50% year over year in the second half of 2026, reflecting sustained customer demand.

AEIS is strengthening its market position through innovative plasma power technologies, including its eVerest and eVoS platforms. These solutions deliver improved yield and throughput for advanced semiconductor manufacturing processes. The company is also gaining traction in system power applications, securing design wins in semiconductor testing, atomic layer deposition and thermal sensing. New product ramps and additional design wins are expected to accelerate revenue growth in 2027 and beyond.

The company's expanding manufacturing footprint is another growth catalyst. AEIS expects to begin generating revenue from its new Thailand facility in the fourth quarter of 2026. Once fully developed, its global manufacturing network is expected to support approximately $5 billion in annual revenue-generating capacity, providing flexibility to address rising semiconductor and data center demand.

AEIS's strong semiconductor revenue growth, expanding product portfolio and improving manufacturing capabilities are expected to boost top-line growth and position it favorably against KLAC and MKSI. For the third quarter of 2026, Advanced Energy expects revenues of $640 million, plus or minus $20 million.

AEIS Faces Stiff Competition

The company is facing stiff competition from companies like KLA and MKS. Both KLA and MKSI are expanding their footprint in the semiconductor market.

KLA is benefiting from strong semiconductor demand, driven by accelerating investments in AI infrastructure, leading-edge foundry/logic, memory and advanced packaging. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, revenues reached a record $3.66 billion, increasing 15% year over year and 7% sequentially. Management attributed the performance to rising AI infrastructure investments and greater process-control intensity across memory and advanced packaging.

MKS is benefiting from rising AI-related investment across semiconductor and advanced packaging markets, with demand broadening through memory, logic, advanced PCBs, photonics, and chemistry equipment. Second-quarter 2026 semiconductor revenues rose 28% year over year to $554 million, with broad-based growth across deposition and etch applications. Management expects third-quarter 2026 semiconductor revenues of $630 million (+/- $15 million), implying more than 50% year-over-year growth, supported by a healthy backlog, NAND upgrades, advanced logic and DRAM demand and design wins in dissolved gas and RF power.

news.Title: If I Could Only Buy 1 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Semiconductor Stock to Buy Before 2027, It Would Be This One
news.Content:
Last week was the worst stretch for chip stocks in over a year. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index dropped more than 11%, a hot inflation print raised the cost of funding every data center on the drawing board, and the impact of worries about CoreWeave 's (NASDAQ: CRWV) debt load spread to every company selling into AI infrastructure.

Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) sank by nearly 17% in five days. And yet, if your goal is to own one AI chip stock heading into 2027, that decline is the reason why you should look into picking up shares of Marvell now rather than later. Even as investors were selling, the company spent the week revealing its most specific, product-level work of the year, and almost nobody noticed because they were watching the tape.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What Marvell announced while its stock was falling

Marvell is not a GPU company. It designs chips that sit around GPUs: the custom accelerators that hyperscalers and AI labs are building for their specific workloads, the optical and copper links that connect thousands of processors into clusters, and the memory controllers that keep those chips fed with data. That is the business the company put on display at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose from Oct. 12 to Oct. 15.

Two announcements from the event stood out to me. On Oct. 12, Marvell unveiled the second generation of its Structera X memory expanders -- chips built to attack what the company calls the "memory wall" in AI inference. The problem is simple: As models get bigger and context windows get longer, GPUs run out of memory before they run out of math. Structera X lets a server bolt on up to 6 terabytes of standard DDR5 memory, share it across four hosts, and compress it on the fly, which the company says cuts time to first token by 40% to 50%. The first generation Structera X is already shipping to hyperscalers, and a Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) hardware engineering director was quoted in the company's release. Test models of the second generation will be available in Q1 2027.

Then, on Oct. 13, Marvell followed by unveiling two 3-nanometer connectivity chips, a 3.2-terabit retimer and a new active electrical cable chip that doubles copper reach to more than six meters between AI servers and switches. Both support UALink, the open standard that non-Nvidia accelerators use to talk to each other. Early samples of both are already available for potential customers.

Story Continues

That sounds like a lot of jargon, so here is the plain version. An AI processor's usefulness will always be limited by the memory it can reach and the capacity of the connections that link it to neighboring chips. The new products Marvell announced last week address both of those bottlenecks: one lets a server strap on far more memory than the GPU came with, so it can handle bigger models without choking, and the other helps racks of accelerators talk to each other over longer, cheaper copper cables without the signal falling apart. These are tools crucial for AI infrastructure, and Marvell is selling them.

Some numbers to consider

On Oct. 6 -- a week before the AI sector rout -- Marvell held its first investor day in years, and management used the event to publicize a target worth reading twice: It's aiming for revenue in the range of $70 billion to $90 billion by its fiscal 2031, up from $8.2 billion in fiscal 2026, with implied non-GAAP earnings above $30 per share . The engine driving it toward those targets is what management calls "XPU attach," the networking, memory, and security chips that get pulled along with every custom accelerator a cloud provider designs.

Big targets deserve some skepticism, and this one assumes 55% to 60% annualized growth for five years. But even if it achieves growth at half that rate, the stock near $228 is cheap against what the company expects to earn. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) saw enough to buy $2 billion of Marvell preferred stock in March, and Nvidia does not make such investments casually.

Other things to consider: Marvell trades at a high trailing earnings ratio; custom chip revenue is lumpy and tied to a few customers; and if hyperscalers pull back due to higher borrowing costs, Marvell will feel the pain before Nvidia does. But last week's sell-off was driven by financing fears, not by any customers walking away, and Marvell kept shipping through it. For anyone able to buy this stock and hold onto it through 2027 or longer, the 17% discount the market just gave it makes it look like a steal.

news.Content:
Google's next TPU chip is reportedly facing delays. Still, GF Securities believes Marvell Technology Inc. If you're weighing MRVL's AI growth potential against short-term uncertainty, these 11 AI stocks are worth a closer look, with Marvell securing the No. 7 spot.

A Delay, Not a Demand Problem

GF Securities says one part of Google's TPU v9 design has slipped by about three weeks, likely due to a redesign. That small delay pushes the timeline back by about a quarter. Tape-out is now scheduled for January 2027, mass production for the second quarter of 2027, and shipments for the first quarter of 2028. Packaging substrate yields are a key obstacle, at just 45% to 50%. However, GF Securities believes it has identified the underlying causes of the problem.

The firm does not see demand as a concern. GF analyst Jeff Pu highlights strong demand for Google's TPUs from both Google itself and external customers, including Anthropic. GF suggests that this external demand may be one reason Gemini 4 is arriving later than expected, as a significant share of Google's TPU v7 went to outside customers in the first half of 2026. The firm identifies MediaTek, rather than Marvell, as facing short-term headwinds. Because the note offers no specific details about Marvell's role in the supply chain, any benefit from the situation appears indirect. However, Jeff Pu's own posts associate v9 with MediaTek, whereas Marvell's potential Google opportunity involves later-generation chips and remains uncertain. As a result, the delay is unlikely to have much direct impact on Marvell. The delay may not change MRVL's short-term outlook, but its AI potential keeps it on investors' radar. Explore our list of 10 AI stocks that could skyrocket, featuring Marvell .

Does Google's Delay Move Marvell's Stock?

At 63x forward earnings, Marvell trades at a 66% premium to its five-year average P/E of 38.02x. So the stock does not look undervalued. Using estimates for the next fiscal year, the multiple comes down to approximately 37x to 40x, near the average, although the two measures use different bases. Investors are paying up for strong earnings growth. EPS is projected to increase 48.59% this fiscal year and 72.58% the next year, with growth accelerating rather than easing.

But that valuation leaves little room for delays. Investors are paying upfront for growth that must arrive on schedule. At its recent investor day, management set long-term targets of roughly $80 billion in revenue and $30 in non-GAAP EPS by calendar year 2030, according to Morningstar. The current premium reflects expectations for that growth. However, Marvell does not seem to generate meaningful revenue from TPU v9, which GF's analyst attributes to MediaTek. As a result, the delay has only a limited, indirect impact on the stock and is not, by itself, a reason to buy.

GF's comments indicate that Marvell's longer-term position in Google's chip supply chain remains intact. But the note does not specify Marvell's role, while rising hedge fund ownership signals broader institutional participation. Still, a 63x multiple on this year's earnings leaves little room for delays. The company needs to deliver on the expected timeline to support its valuation.

news.Title: Is Marvell Technology a Millionaire-Maker Stock?
news.Content:
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) is deeply involved in artificial intelligence infrastructure, with its optical chips, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), data storage controllers, and CXL memory products. This broad portfolio of products explains why Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said back in June that he expects Marvell Technology to be the next $1 trillion company.

Given its current market cap of around $215 million, that prediction implies a nearly 5x return from current levels, a gain that could help mint many new millionaires, and the fundamentals certainly look promising. Here's what investors should know.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Marvell's long-term deal with Alphabet gives it a massive backlog

Marvell Technology is already doing well. In its fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended Aug. 1, the company delivered 37% year-over-year revenue growth, with "AI-related bookings remain[ing] exceptionally robust," according to Marvell Technology CEO Matt Murphy. He also expects AI revenue to accelerate further in fiscal 2027, prompting the company to raise its guidance for fiscal 2027 and 2028.

Moreover, after that quarter ended (but before its report came out), the company announced a big expansion of its AI chip deal with Alphabet . It amounts to $120 billion over roughly six and a half years, and that business arrangement starts in Marvell's fiscal 2029.

Marvell Technology will continue to strengthen its market position in the meantime, and if it can land big deals like that with other tech giants, it could see an extended rally. Marvell Technology generated $2.74 billion in sales in its fiscal Q2 while boosting net profit margins, and its guidance for the upcoming quarter implies 15% sequential revenue growth at the midpoint.

A high valuation is the price of entry

Although Marvell Technology has several attractive catalysts ahead of it, the stock isn't cheap. It trades at a forward P/E ratio of 62. Other chipmakers such as Broadcom and Nvidia offer cheaper valuations and solid growth prospects. Furthermore, those two companies are exhibiting higher revenue growth rates than Marvell Technology.

While Nvidia and Broadcom look more attractive if you only consider next year, Marvell Technology may be the better choice when considered over a five-year time horizon. Its big deal with Alphabet will contribute roughly $5 billion per quarter in sales once it starts, and that's almost two times Marvell Technology's Q2 FY27 revenue.

Story Continues

Marvell Technology is still of a size where a single new contract of that magnitude can change the investment thesis in the stock overnight. Nvidia is on its way to more than $100 billion in quarterly revenue, so it would need multiple large contracts to sustain meaningful growth. Marvell Technology is well-positioned to gain market share as optical chips and ASICs gain traction. A few more major contracts could spark a rally that lifts its market cap closer to Jensen Huang's $1 trillion prediction.

news.Title: The AI Sell-Off Continues—These 3 Stocks Keep Raising Guidance Anyway
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in Lumentum Holdings Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

AI infrastructure stocks are selling off even as suppliers report sold-out capacity, rising guidance and multi-year backlogs, according to TradeSmith's Lucas Downey.

Lumentum, Dell Technologies and Everpure each show falling share prices alongside rising earnings estimates, compressing forward valuations and creating a widening gap between price and fundamentals.

Downey views the decline as driven by investor positioning and seasonal weakness rather than broken fundamentals, and says upcoming earnings revisions will determine when the sell-off ends.

The artificial intelligence (AI) trade finally cracked. After months of resilience while utilities, real estate and consumer discretionary names took a beating, the market's favorite growth story is now the one getting sold, and investors sitting on big gains are rushing to lock them in.

The fear has a familiar shape. Earlier this year, software stocks were written off as AI roadkill, and the slide dragged on for roughly 60 days. Many of those same names have since reclaimed all-time highs, because the earnings never broke the way the headlines said they would.

→ These 3 Green Stocks Have a Growth Story That Goes Far Beyond Washington

That's the tension now. Prices are falling across AI infrastructure while the companies building it keep raising guidance, reporting sold-out capacity and pointing to backlogs that stretch for years. When price and fundamentals move in opposite directions, valuations compress, and that gap is where opportunity tends to surface.

AI Sell-Off Looks Driven by Positioning, Not Broken Fundamentals

The selling looks more like positioning than a verdict on the businesses, per Lucas Downey, editor at TradeSmith. Many investors came into the slide underweight in the interest-rate-sensitive stocks that look most attractive as rates come down, while sitting on large embedded gains in AI. Selling the winners is the fastest way to rebalance, while some heavily leveraged investors may have no choice but to sell.

→ The AI Sell-Off Continues—These 3 Stocks Keep Raising Guidance Anyway

Seasonality adds friction. Late September has historically been weak, and midterm election years tend to run volatile as investors handicap the fight for Congress. Downey sees signs of capitulation and puts a potential bottom in the next couple of weeks, with earnings season the likely catalyst. By his read, further downside remains on the table.

Story Continues

The deeper worry, though, is whether hyperscalers can keep paying for the build-out as data center costs climb. Downey points to what suppliers are reporting. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML) have described demand as strong and, in many cases, accelerating, and committed contracts stretch out for years.

→ Tesla's Roadster Reveal Hints at 2 Much Bigger Moves

Optical Components Sell Out Into 2029 as Earnings Estimates Rise

Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ: LITE) makes the lasers and optical components that move enormous volumes of data at high speed inside AI data centers. As demand runs into the limits of materials and manufacturing capacity, those parts become a bottleneck.

CEO Michael Hurlston has said the company is sold out of optical components for AI servers through early 2029. Sales over the last 12 months came in just over $3 billion, and estimates cited by Downey call for about $6.3 billion over the next 12 months, approaching $10 billion the year after. Earnings per share (EPS) estimates sit at $21.70 for fiscal 2027 and $47.88 for fiscal 2029.

A roughly 400% gain over the past year is exactly what makes latecomers nervous. But the stock has dropped about 15% in a week, and with estimates rising as the price falls, the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio has compressed to about 42. The market is pricing a momentum unwind. Another round of upward estimate revisions could change that, so earnings follow-through is the thing to watch.

AI Server Demand Fuels a Blowout Beat and Raise

Dell Technologies (NYSE: DELL) spent decades as the personal computer brand everyone knew. Its infrastructure business, spanning servers, storage, networking equipment and software, has turned it into a cornerstone of the AI build-out, and the stock has climbed more than 200% in a year.

The latest quarter was a beat and a raise. Per Downey, Dell guided third-quarter EPS to $6.50 against estimates of $4.46 and revenue to $49 billion against a consensus just above $41 billion, then lifted its fiscal 2027 outlook. In his view, the stock effectively repriced on that report.

A surprise that big raises the bar, and priced-for-perfection risk is real. The counterweight is valuation. With forward estimates climbing while shares slide, the forward P/E has fallen to around 18, below the broader market. The market is pricing an AI hardware hangover. Next quarter's results are what to watch, since they test whether this guidance was a one-off.

Enterprise Flash Storage Lands Hyperscale Wins and a Higher Outlook

The smallest of the three is Everpure (NYSE: P), which builds all-flash data storage systems, the infrastructure companies use to manage data and run AI workloads, at enterprise scale. Management had flagged hyperscale customer wins, and those are starting to show up in results.

Everpure reiterated guidance and raised its preliminary fiscal 2028 outlook to $7.15 billion at the midpoint, against a Street estimate of $6.2 billion. That's a message of acceleration, not slowdown. The stock also scores an 88 on TradeSmith's proprietary Quantum Edge system, which blends fundamental and technical factors into a single rating; TradeSmith reads that as a high-quality stock.

Storage and memory names such as Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) have been caught in the same downdraft, even as workloads keep growing. A smaller company brings bigger swings, and stocks don't move in straight lines. What could change sentiment is continued upward movement in analysts' EPS forecasts, and that trend is the one to watch.

Earnings Revisions Hold the Key to the End of the AI Sell-Off

Lumentum, Dell and Everpure sit at different links in the same chain: optics that move the data, servers that process it and storage that holds it. What connects them is a widening gap—falling share prices against rising forward numbers.

The risk is that the hyperscaler spending debate drags on, flows stay negative, and the smaller names take the hardest hits, much like software's two-month grind. The upside is that sold-out capacity, multi-year backlogs and raised guidance are company-reported numbers, and compressed valuations leave room to recover if earnings season confirms them.

None of this requires calling the exact bottom. It does require hyperscalers to keep spending and these companies to deliver on guidance already issued. Stay focused on earnings revisions, because that's what moves these stocks once the selling runs its course.

news.Title: Oracle Slumped 9% Amid a Tech Selloff and AI Buildout Concerns. Investors Should Cautiously Buy the Dip.
news.Content:
Oracle's (ORCL) artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions come with a hefty price tag, and investors are now questioning how much risk they should accept to fund it. Shares tumbled nearly 9% in a single session on Oct. 14 as a broader technology selloff put the financing of AI infrastructure under scrutiny.

The pressure extended across the sector. CoreWeave (CRWV) dropped more than 15% as a selloff in its corporate bonds heightened financing concerns, while Marvell Technology (MRVL) lost more than 8%.

More News from Barchart

No 'Example Anywhere on the Planet': Billionaire Kevin O'Leary's Utah Data Center Could Use Enough Electricity to Power 16 Million People

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

Hotter-than-expected inflation data added further pressure. U.S. annual inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, raising the prospect of higher interest rates and more expensive financing for the industry's massive infrastructure buildout.

For Oracle, this strikes at the core of its investment case. The sharp selloff, therefore, raises a more fundamental question. Has the decline created an attractive opportunity to invest in the AI expansion? Or is the lower share price a warning of the financial risks? Let's find out.

Oracle's Financial Check

Based in Austin, Texas, Oracle is valued at approximately $387 billion by market capitalization and provides enterprise databases, business applications, and cloud infrastructure for organizations managing data and deploying AI. Beyond its established software business, the company is expanding computing capacity to serve customers requiring infrastructure for demanding AI workloads.

ORCL stock closed on Oct. 16 at $128.23 per share. The stock has declined 33% year-to-date (YTD) and 55% for the past 52 weeks.

At 19.7 times trailing earnings versus the roughly 32 times sector median, Oracle looks cheaper on earnings but pricier on sales at 6 times versus about 3.5 times for the sector. Oracle's $2 annualized dividend also yields approximately 1.49%.

Oracle released first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings on Sept. 10. Revenue rose 30% year-over-year (YOY) to $19.35 billion, beating the $19.1 billion analyst estimate. Adjusted EPS also increased 30% YOY to $1.92 and exceeded the $1.74 consensus estimate.

Story Continues

That earnings strength extended to operating results. Oracle reported adjusted operating income of $8.15 billion against expectations of $7.8 billion. This was a 4.5% beat, with an adjusted operating margin of roughly 42%.

Cloud infrastructure drove much of the revenue growth, jumping 121% to $7.4 billion. Cloud applications revenue increased 10% to $4.2 billion, while software revenue fell 3% to $5.5 billion.

To support that cloud expansion, the company delivered 850 megawatts of additional data-center capacity and more than 300,000 GPUs. Those GPU deliveries nearly tripled the preceding quarter's total.

Oracle also added more than $30 billion in AI cloud contracts during the quarter. This pushed remaining performance obligations (RPO) to $664 billion, up $209 billion YOY.

However, the expansion continued to weigh on cash flow. Free cash flow fell to -$5.4 billion from -$1.87 billion in the previous quarter.

Oracle's Next Growth Drivers

Oracle's latest product launches and partnerships show where its next phase of growth could come from and what shareholders will help finance. On Sept. 29, Oracle introduced Fusion Claw with 25 new applications, expanding its agentic application portfolio to 75. The technology combines AI reasoning with precise enterprise computation to automate complex tasks under customer-defined controls.

Infrastructure security is advancing, too. On Oct. 13, Oracle, Microsoft (MSFT), and Marvell established an Open Compute Project working group targeting NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware security. Their proposed server-integrated security module would protect cryptographic keys where workloads run, reducing network dependence and supporting regulatory compliance.

Oracle also launched Nexus Case Flow and Nexus Reach on Sept. 29 for financial crime investigations. These offerings target compliance workloads where efficiency must coexist with accountability.

That same day, NetApp (NTAP) and Oracle announced OCI NetApp Storage Service, with general availability planned within 12 months. Its ONTAP capabilities would help customers migrate databases, enterprise applications, and AI workloads without substantially redesigning existing storage operations.

However, expansion brings obligations beyond hardware. On Oct. 2, Oracle committed to absorbing approximately $300 million in rising Point Beach nuclear energy costs, benefiting over 1 million Wisconsin utility customers. The company's related Project Lighthouse development projects more than $11 billion in local economic benefits, 4,000 construction jobs over three years, and 1,000 ongoing positions.

These initiatives give Oracle more ways to win cloud business, but they also add to the spending shareholders must weigh. The key is how quickly those commitments translate into revenue and stronger cash flow.

Wall Street's Case for Oracle

Oracle's next earnings report is scheduled for Dec. 9. Analysts expect November-quarter EPS of $1.57, down 19% from $1.95 a year earlier.

Despite that projected decline, Citi sees an opportunity. In August, the firm placed Oracle on a 90-day upside catalyst watch, maintaining a "Buy" rating and a $330 price target. Citi's thesis rests on AI infrastructure demand supporting stronger cloud growth, pricing, and profitability. Citi also identified earnings and an upcoming investor day as potential catalysts.

JPMorgan offered a more measured endorsement in August, retaining an "Overweight" rating while cutting its target to $200 from $210. Analyst Samik Chatterjee noted aggressive infrastructure spending and capital requirements but maintained that Oracle could capitalize on AI expansion.

That optimism extends beyond Citi and JPMorgan. Across 43 analysts with coverage, ORCL stock holds a consensus "Strong Buy" rating. The average price target of $242.22 implies potential upside of approximately 86% from current levels.

Conclusion

Oracle looks more like a cautious buy than a stock to avoid. Strong cloud growth supports the opportunity, but heavy spending and negative free cash flow warrant smaller positions rather than aggressive buying. A gradual recovery looks more likely than a quick rebound, provided demand holds and financing remains manageable. The next earnings report will need to show that expansion is producing better financial results. Buying shares gradually makes sense here, but chasing a bounce before cash flow improves would be premature.

news.Title: If Apple Cuts iPhone Units in 2027, This Stock Could Be a Big Loser
news.Content:
Apple (AAPL) is reportedly asking several key suppliers to scale back component production for its flagship devices, as higher retail prices driven by rising memory chip costs appear to be cooling consumer demand. And if iPhone sales lose steam, the ripple effects could reach far beyond Apple itself.

Take Cirrus Logic (CRUS), for instance. The semiconductor company relies heavily on Apple, which contributes the lion's share of its revenue, according to KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh. With Apple reportedly taking a more cautious approach to iPhone production, Vinh sees a risk that unit sales could stay flat or slip slightly in 2027, dampening Cirrus Logic's growth prospects. That concern prompted him to downgrade CRUS stock, adding to the pressure on shares.

Cirrus supplies custom audio and mixed-signal chips used in smartphones, making it particularly sensitive to changes in Apple's production plans. With its potential PC growth opportunity also facing delays, investors have more than one reason to pay attention. So, if Apple trims iPhone production in 2027, could Cirrus Logic be among the biggest losers? Let's take a closer look.

About Cirrus Logic Stock

Founded in 1984, Cirrus Logic is a fabless semiconductor company headquartered in Austin, Texas, with offices across the United States, Europe, and Asia. The company designs high-performance analog, mixed-signal, and audio digital signal processing (DSP) integrated circuits used in smartphones, tablets, laptops, smartwatches, automotive entertainment systems, and other consumer electronics.

Its product portfolio includes smart codecs, amplifiers, haptics and sensing solutions, camera controllers, and battery and power ICs. With approximately 1,717 employees worldwide, Cirrus Logic focuses on power efficiency, audio quality, and innovative chip designs. The company has a market capitalization of around $5.4 billion.

Cirrus Logic's stock started the year on a high note, climbing to $180.42 in May 2026 as strong fiscal 2026 results and optimism around the semiconductor sector gave investors plenty to cheer about. But that enthusiasm has since faded. By Oct. 15, shares had tumbled to a 52-week low of $105.10, down 40% from their peak. CRUS stock has lost 14% over the past year and 35% over six months, with recent losses reflecting softer PC market expectations and concerns about its heavy reliance on Apple, its largest customer.

Story Continues

Things got more interesting after Cirrus announced its acquisition of Italy-based INVENTVM Semiconductor on Oct. 6. The deal aims to expand its technology portfolio and reach new markets, but the financial terms remain undisclosed, and management expects no material revenue impact. That may explain why investors have not warmed up to the deal just yet, as they weigh its long-term potential against the lack of an immediate financial boost.

Technically, CRUS stock shows signs of stabilization, but the picture remains shaky. The 14-day RSI has bounced back from oversold territory to around 34, though it is still below the neutral mark. Meanwhile, the MACD line remains below its signal line, with a negative histogram pointing to continued bearish momentum.

On the valuation front, CRUS stock looks relatively affordable, trading at 12.88 times forward adjusted earnings and 2.68 times forward sales. Both multiples sit below the stock's five-year averages and those of its sector peers, making its current valuation worth a closer look.

A Closer Look at Cirrus Logic's Q1 Earnings Report

In August, Cirrus Logic released its Q1 2027 earnings report and started the year on a strong note, posting record first-quarter revenue and earnings. That's largely due to healthy demand for custom chips used in premium smartphones. The company also made progress on its broader growth plans, although its PC business faced a few speed bumps.

Revenue rose 12.9% year-over-year (YoY) to $460 million, almost in line with Wall Street's expectations. Sales also increased 2.5% sequentially as stronger shipments of smartphone components lifted results. Demand for custom-boosted amplifiers and smart codecs remained strong, helping the company deliver record quarterly earnings. Adjusted EPS climbed 21.9% annually to $1.84, beating analysts' estimates. However, previously anticipated pricing reductions partly offset the revenue gains. Cirrus remains heavily reliant on its biggest customer, Apple, which accounted for 90% of first-quarter revenue.

Beyond smartphones, Cirrus is working to expand its footprint in AI-enabled PCs and other markets. Interest in its latest low-power smart codec for AI PCs remains strong, with multiple customers working on designs expected to launch next calendar year. However, supply constraints involving a key industry platform, memory and other components, along with delayed PC launches, have pushed expected growth further out.

As a result, management lowered its fiscal 2027 PC revenue expectations, describing the challenges as timing issues rather than a change in the long-term opportunity. Several customers have also announced PCs based on Nvidia's (NVDA) RTX Spark platform that are expected to ship later this year with Cirrus amplifiers and codecs.

The company is also advancing its next-generation camera controller and smart power IC for 3D sensing, while a newly taped-out high-performance analog front-end component targeting metrology applications adds to its general market portfolio.

Cirrus ended the quarter with $1.2 billion in cash and investments and no debt. Operating cash flow reached $64.1 million, while free cash flow came in at $48.6 million, representing an 11% margin. The company repurchased about 211,000 shares for $34.5 million during the quarter and bought another 359,000 shares for $50.5 million after quarter-end. Management continues to prioritize investments in the business, followed by acquisitions and share buybacks, with no near-term dividend planned.

Looking ahead, Cirrus expects Q2 revenue between $510 million and $570 million, with the midpoint implying 17% sequential growth but roughly 4% YoY decline. GAAP gross margin is projected at 52% to 54%. While smartphone demand remains a key support, investors will be watching whether Cirrus can turn its growing AI-PC pipeline into meaningful revenue as supply constraints ease.

Cirrus Logic is gearing up to report its second-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Wednesday, Nov. 4, after the closing bell, and Wall Street will be watching to see how the chipmaker is holding up. Analysts expect revenue to come in at around $540.4 million, while EPS is projected to slip nearly 16% YoY to $2.11. Looking further ahead, fiscal 2027 earnings are expected to fall 8.9% annually to $7.24 per share. There could be some relief in fiscal 2028, though, with EPS projected to rebound 4.7% YoY to $7.58.

What Do Analysts Think About CRUS Stock?

KeyBanc downgraded CRUS stock to a "Sector Weight" from an "Overweight," citing its heavy reliance on Apple and delayed diversification prospects. Analyst John Vinh noted that Apple's cuts to TSMC (TSM) wafer starts, equivalent to 15 million to 20 million iPhones, suggest weaker iPhone volumes in 2027.

With roughly 90% of Cirrus Logic's revenue tied to Apple, Vinh sees limited growth over the next six to 12 months. Meanwhile, elevated memory prices and an expected 10% to 15% decline in PC shipments this year could delay its PC diversification plans, despite meaningful share gains in the segment. KeyBanc also questioned Cirrus' unsuccessful Synaptics (SYNA) acquisition bid from a strategic standpoint.

Analysts have been moderately bullish about Cirrus Logic, with seven who cover the stock giving a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating. Among them, three suggest a "Strong Buy," three are playing it safe with a "Hold" rating, while the remaining one has a "Strong Sell."

The mean price target of $123.20 indicates CRUS has an upside potential of 13%, and the high target of $200 suggests that the stock could rise as much as 83% from the current price level.

news.Title: Arm vs. Lumentum: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
news.Content:
As artificial intelligence (AI) pushes computing power and data transmission to new limits, investors are weighing different paths to growth. Is Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) or Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) the better choice today?

Arm creates the foundational blueprints for the world's most energy-efficient processors. Lumentum provides the optical components that allow data centers to communicate at lightning speeds. Both companies are central to the infrastructure of modern computing, but they operate with vastly different business models and financial profiles.

The case for Arm

Arm designs and licenses central processing units (CPUs) and other systems used in everything from smartphones to high-performance data centers. Rather than manufacturing chips, the company earns revenue through licensing fees and royalties on every chip sold. This model enables high scalability and profit margins in the semiconductor industry .

In fiscal 2026 (ending in March), Arm's revenue reached $4.9 billion. This represents growth of nearly 23% compared to the prior year. Net income was roughly $698 million, though the net margin decreased slightly from roughly 16% in the previous year to about 14%.

As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating the company has very little debt relative to its net equity. The current ratio is roughly 5.3x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations.

Trailing-12-month (TTM) free cash flow was $1.5 billion through the June quarter, but note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Lumentum

Lumentum manufactures optical and photonic products essential to cloud data centers and telecommunications networks. In its latest fiscal year ended June 27, 2026, Lumentum revealed that Customer A accounted for approximately 26.6% of revenue while Customer B accounted for roughly 15%. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as the loss of either client would be significant.

For fiscal 2026, the company reported revenue of $3 billion, which was an increase of about 83% over the prior year. Despite this massive top-line growth, the company reported a net loss of approximately $6.9 billion, although its operating profit (earnings before interest and taxes) was $525 million. The $6.9 billion net loss was due to a $7.7 billion non-recurring loss on debt extinguishment.

Story Continues

According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.4x. The current ratio is nearly 1.7x, indicating about $1.70 in short-term assets for every $1.00 of short-term debt.

TTM free cash flow for the period was roughly $300 million. However, stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Risk profile comparison

Arm faces intense competition from established rivals and open-source alternatives. If major tech companies decide to design their own architectures rather than paying licensing fees, the company could see its market share erode. Additionally, the business relies on continued growth in the mobile and data center markets, and any slowdown in hardware upgrades would impact its royalty income.

Lumentum is highly dependent on a small number of customers for a significant portion of its sales, and many relationships lack long-term volume commitments. The company is also subject to complex trade policies and export controls, specifically regarding operations in China. Competition from global firms such as IPG Photonics and Viavi Solutions exerts constant pressure on pricing and operating margins.

Valuation comparison

Lumentum appears to be the more value-oriented choice as it trades at a significant discount to its peer across both sales and future earnings estimates.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

Arm is a great business that generates high margins from royalties and licensing fees. It would be a solid chip stock to own, but Lumentum offers better value right now.

Analysts expect Arm to grow earnings at a 25% annualized rate in the coming years. However, Lumentum is expected to deliver 132% annualized growth, as the business scales and expands margins. Lumentum is benefiting from data centers shifting to optical connectivity for AI workloads. Revenue surged 109% year over year in the recent quarter, marking the eighth consecutive quarter of growth and signaling strong momentum that may not be fully reflected in the stock's valuation right now.

Arm is benefiting from the growing demand for CPUs, and its expertise in designing power-efficient chips could help it gain market share in the data center market.

Both companies are meeting demand at crucial chokepoints for AI, and they both face comparable risks. But it's difficult for me to pass up the huge discrepancy between each stock's PEG ratios. I would buy Lumentum since it's growing much faster than Arm and commands a much lower premium for future earnings growth.

Marvell designs custom chips for the companies running large data centres. When a cloud provider wants its own processor rather than a standard one, Marvell is among the small group of firms that can design it. As per CNN, of the analysts covering the stock, 92% rate it a buy. The other 8% do not, and since the bull case has been made everywhere, the more interesting question is what the holdouts see.

The Case Almost Everyone Agrees With:

The growth is not in doubt. Revenue rose 36.5% in the most recent quarter, and the shares are up 174% over twelve months.

The work itself is sticky. A customer that commits to a custom design cannot switch supplier without starting the engineering again, which takes years. That buys Marvell a position no standard chip vendor gets.

What the Minority Is Weighing:

The first thing is the price. Marvell trades at 62.11 times what analysts expect next year, which is by some distance the most demanding multiple on our list of ten.

The second is profitability. Operating margin runs at 16.68%. That is respectable for most industries and modest next to the other companies selling into artificial intelligence, several of which earn three or four times as much on every dollar of sales.

The third is who the customers are. Custom silicon work comes from a handful of very large technology firms, and the stickiness that protects Marvell also means a lost design is lost for the life of the product. The same feature that reads as a moat is the thing that makes each decision matter so much.

What the Gap Is Really Measuring:

The holdouts are not arguing that the business is in trouble. They are arguing about what it is worth.

That is the honest shape of the disagreement here. Nobody doubts the growth or the position. The question is whether a company earning these margins should carry a multiple several times what its larger and more profitable peers do.

Conclusion:

The minority view is not a bear case about the business. It is a bear case about the price, which is a different thing and easier to be right about. Marvell is winning work that is hard to take away and growing quickly on the back of it. The margins it earns are ordinary by the standards of its own industry, and the multiple is not. Decide which of those two facts you are buying, because the multiple assumes only one of them matters.
